title: SHA-256 content hashing of records (foundational)
description: Every record is hashed with SHA-256 as defined in FIPS 180-4, and the digest is stored alongside the record as its integrity fingerprint. SHA-256 is used because it is collision-resistant in practice and universally supported, so fingerprints can be checked with any standard toolchain. Any single-bit change in the record produces a completely different digest, which is exactly the tamper-evidence property the verifier needs. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
import hashlib
rec = '{"id":"JAH-AT58-000001","title":"hash check"}'
d = hashlib.sha256(rec.encode()).hexdigest()
print('digest:', d[:32] + '...')
tampered = rec.replace('hash', 'haxh')
print('tamper detected:', hashlib.sha256(tampered.encode()).hexdigest() != d)
provenance: Public computer-science methods literature (Data Integrity Verifier practice); cross-checked against standard references, 2026-10-21.

title: Merkle tree batch verification (foundational)
description: For large collections, records are arranged as leaves of a Merkle tree: each parent node hashes the concatenation of its children, up to a single root digest. Verifying the whole archive then costs one root comparison instead of one hash per record, and a mismatch can be localized to a single leaf in logarithmic steps. This is the same structure that underpins version-control and blockchain integrity proofs. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
import hashlib
def H(x): return hashlib.sha256(x.encode()).hexdigest()
leaves = ['rec1','rec2','rec3','rec4']
lvl = [H(l) for l in leaves]
while len(lvl) > 1:
    lvl = [H(lvl[i] + lvl[i+1]) for i in range(0, len(lvl), 2)]
print('merkle root:', lvl[0][:24] + '...')
print('leaves verified with 1 root comparison')
provenance: Public computer-science methods literature (Data Integrity Verifier practice); cross-checked against standard references, 2026-10-21.

title: Structural validity against schema (foundational)
description: Beyond hashes, the verifier checks that each record parses and conforms to its declared schema: required fields present, types correct, enumerations within range. A record can hash correctly and still be structurally broken, for example a JSON file truncated mid-write that still has a recorded hash from before truncation. Schema validation catches corruption that cryptography alone cannot see. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
provenance: Public computer-science methods literature (Data Integrity Verifier practice); cross-checked against standard references, 2026-10-21.

title: Checksum audit sweep across chunks (foundational)
description: On a schedule, the verifier sweeps every chunk file, recomputes digests, and compares them against the manifest's recorded values. Failures are classified as bit-rot, truncation, or replacement, and the affected chunk is quarantined for repair from a replica. Sweep results feed a rolling integrity score for the whole archive. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
provenance: Public computer-science methods literature (Data Integrity Verifier practice); cross-checked against standard references, 2026-10-21.

title: Tamper-evident integrity report (foundational)
description: Each sweep ends in a signed integrity report: counts of records checked, pass rate, failures with chunk and record identifiers, and the verifier version. The report itself is hashed and appended to an append-only log, so the history of integrity checks cannot be rewritten after the fact. Operators read this log, not ad-hoc claims, when they need to trust the archive. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
import hashlib, json
report = {'checked': 1500, 'passed': 1498, 'failed': ['c2#118'], 'verifier': 'jahdb-integrity-1.0'}
blob = json.dumps(report, sort_keys=True)
report['report_hash'] = hashlib.sha256(blob.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
print('integrity report:', json.dumps(report))
provenance: Public computer-science methods literature (Data Integrity Verifier practice); cross-checked against standard references, 2026-10-21.
